content: Infections caused by Trichomonas vaginalis in newborns are rare but have been documented. Non-sexual transmission of T. vaginalis is uncommon, though it has been reported in young girls who deny any sexual activity. In such cases, transmission has been linked to contaminated moist washcloths, toilet seats, specula, shared bathing water, and shared bathing implements. However, when T. vaginalis is detected in young girls, it is crucial to carefully assess for the possibility of sexual abuse. Clinical Features of T. vaginalis Infection Approximately 50–85% of women with T. vaginalis infections are asymptomatic. Among these, 30–50% may develop symptoms within six months. Symptomatic women often report abnormal vaginal discharge, typically described as yellow and purulent. About half of symptomatic women also experience vulvar itching. On examination, vulvar erythema and edema may be observed. Speculum examination may reveal a yellow or greenish vaginal discharge, sometimes frothy in appearance, along with vaginal mucosal erythema indicative of vaginitis. The cervix may exhibit punctate hemorrhages, known as strawberry cervix, which, although uncommon, is highly suggestive of T. vaginalis infection. In men, over 50% of T. vaginalis infections are asymptomatic, likely due to a low parasite burden. Symptomatic men may present with clear or mucopurulent urethral discharge and dysuria. The incubation period for T. vaginalis-induced urethritis in men is estimated to be 3–9 days. Diagnosis of T. vaginalis Four main diagnostic methods are available: wet mount microscopy, antigen detection assays, culture, and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs). Wet mount microscopy is quick, inexpensive, and easy to perform but requires the slide to be examined within 10 minutes of sample collection to detect motile trichomonads. Non-motile cells are unreliable for diagnosis. Antigen detection assays are limited by the need for specialized equipment and cost, and many are designed for symptomatic women only. Culture has a sensitivity of about 70% compared to NAATs and can take up to seven days, making it less commonly used. NAATs have the highest sensitivity and have improved the detection of T. vaginalis, even in asymptomatic individuals, allowing for treatment to prevent further transmission. Vaginal swabs are the preferred sample for women, while urine and urethral swabs are used for men. Integrating T. vaginalis testing into existing NAAT-based programs for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis is recommended. Treatment of T. vaginalis The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends the following treatments for adults and adolescents, including pregnant women: Metronidazole 400–500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. For cases where adherence to multiple doses is a concern, a single dose of metronidazole 2 g orally or tinidazole 2 g orally (except during pregnancy) may be used. Sexual partners of individuals with T. vaginalis infection should also be treated, either after testing and screening for other sexually transmitted infections (STIs) or presumptively. Although T. vaginalis infection in men is often considered benign and self-limiting, it is important to assess and treat male partners of infected women, as many are also infected. Mycoplasma genitalium (M. genitalium) M. genitalium is a sexually transmitted bacterium with a flask-shaped structure and the smallest known genome capable of self-replication. It lacks a cell wall, making it resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics like penicillins and cephalosporins. It is commonly found in the human urogenital tract and has been associated with non-gonococcal urethritis, epididymitis, and chronic prostatitis in men, as well as cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and bacterial vaginosis in women. It has also been identified as a risk factor for HIV infection. Diagnosis of M. genitalium Routine screening for M. genitalium is not recommended except in cases of recurrent symptomatic episodes. Diagnosis is best achieved using molecular techniques like PCR, ideally with macrolide resistance testing. Culture methods are labor-intensive and take months, making them impractical. There are no effective serological or rapid diagnostic tests currently available. Treatment of M. genitalium Treatment should be guided by resistance profiles or local surveillance data. WHO recommendations include: In settings with high macrolide resistance: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, followed by moxifloxacin 400 mg orally once daily for 7 days. In settings with low macrolide resistance: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, followed by azithromycin 1 g orally on day 1, then 500 mg once daily for 3 days. If azithromycin or moxifloxacin is unavailable or resistance is high, alternative options include minocycline, sitafloxacin, or pristinamycin. Vulvovaginal Candidiasis (VVC) VVC affects 70–75% of women at least once in their lifetime, with Candida albicans responsible for 90% of cases. Symptoms include vulvar itching, burning, soreness, and irritation, often accompanied by a thick, white, curd-like discharge. Recurrent VVC is defined as three or more symptomatic episodes within 12 months. Diagnosis of VVC Microscopy of vaginal secretions can demonstrate Candida species, and culture methods are recommended for isolation. Molecular tests exist but are not yet widely used for VVC diagnosis. Treatment of VVC WHO recommendations for treatment include: Fluconazole 150–200 mg orally as a single dose. Intravaginal options such as clotrimazole, miconazole, econazole, or nystatin. For pregnant women, intravaginal clotrimazole or nystatin is preferred. Treatment choice may depend on patient preference for oral or intravaginal administration and cost considerations. Bacterial Vaginosis (BV) BV is the most common cause of vaginal discharge globally among women of childbearing age. It is characterized by a dysbiosis of the vaginal microbiome, often resulting in malodorous discharge. Prevalence varies by region, ranging from 23% to 29% among women of reproductive age.
